Denver property tax is billed by the offices named below.

Who bills what in Denver

  • Denver Assessor's Office handles assessment.
  • Denver Treasury Division bills and collects the tax.

Due dates

Per Denver Treasury: first half due last day of February, second half June 15, full payment April 30; dates falling on a weekend/holiday move to next business day.. See the official page.

Challenging your assessment

Protest deadline for current year by any method is June 8 (or next business day); file in writing, in person or online per instructions on Notice of Valuation. If you disagree with the Board's decision you may appeal to the State Board of Assessment Appeals, District Court, or binding arbitration.. See the official page.

Tax rate

We could not confirm the current Denver rate on an opened page, so we do not state one.

Local notes

  • Colorado: the elected county Assessor values property and the elected county Treasurer (often also Public Trustee) collects taxes for all taxing districts in the county; cities do not assess or collect.
  • Denver is a consolidated city and county; the Denver Assessor values and the Denver Treasury Division (Department of Finance) collects.
  • Census Vintage 2025 population 740613; primary county Denver County (Census SUMLEV 157).
Behind on Denver property tax?
We buy Denver houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.
Get My Cash Offer →

Denver by the numbers

Denver has roughly 713,734 residents in the Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey, and ranks number 1 by population among the 34 co places in this guide. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $586,700 here, which is 7% above the middle figure for the 34 co places. About 51% of households rent, so 49% own; the co median for these places is 66% owner-occupied. Homes here were typically built in 1974, so the median house is about 49 years old. These numbers describe Denver as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.
